author: Carlos Martinez
title: Road America on iRacing: Managing the Long Straights and Blind Crests
description: My corner-by-corner notes and setup approach for Road America on iRacing, raced from a MOZA R9 direct-drive rig.

sections.p: I run all of this from a fixed-aluminium-extrusion cockpit with a ~MOZA R9 direct drive wheelbase and ~MOZA CRP2 load-cell pedals — no motion, no fancy paint, just a rig built to be honest about what the car is doing. This week it's Road America — one of the tracks I keep coming back to on iRacing, and one where the corner-by-corner details matter more than most. I've raced enough laps here across enough car classes that I've stopped thinking of it as one lap and started thinking of it as a handful of separate problems strung together, which is honestly how I'd recommend approaching any new track once you're past the total-beginner stage.

None of what follows is a substitute for laps. iRacing's tire model and each car's balance shift enough between builds and seasons that exact setup numbers go stale fast — what doesn't go stale is which corners at Road America punish which mistakes, and that's what I'm actually trying to hand off here.

Before I get into setup or technique, it's worth walking the layout once with fresh eyes, because most of the time lost at a new track comes from not knowing what's coming next rather than from any actual driving mistake.

list: Turn 5 (the Kink) — flat or near-flat in most GT3s, but the first time it isn't, it's a big accident
Canada Corner (Turn 6) — a heavy braking zone that decides your run down the following straight
The Carousel — a long, off-camber-feeling right-hander that punishes an early throttle application
Turn 14 — the final corner, slow and tight, setting up the long run to the line

sections.p: I'd genuinely recommend doing a slow, no-pressure lap or two just looking around before pushing for pace — glance at the runoff, the curbing, and where the track actually widens versus where it only looks like it does. A surprising amount of confidence at Road America comes from simply knowing the track's shape well enough that you're not making decisions on the fly anymore.

sections.h2: Where I set up the car differently here

sections.p: My starting point for Road America is never a totally clean-sheet setup — I take whatever baseline I'm running that week for the car class and adjust from there based on what this specific layout demands.

list: I run less downforce here than almost anywhere else on the calendar — Road America is mostly about straight-line speed between the corners
Gearing gets stretched to make the most of the long straights rather than optimizing for any single corner
Brake bias comes forward slightly for Canada Corner, which is a hard, high-speed stop

sections.p: I'd treat all of this as a starting point rather than a final answer. Setup work on iRacing rewards small, deliberate changes tested one at a time far more than it rewards big swings based on a feeling — change one thing, run a handful of laps, and actually compare lap times and how the car felt rather than just going on instinct.

sections.h2: A practice session plan that actually works

olist: Run three or four laps at a moderate pace just to build a mental map of the corners before pushing for time
Push for a genuinely fast lap once the tires and track feel warmed in, and note exactly where you felt like you left time on the table
Adjust one setup parameter based on that feeling, then run another push lap to see if it actually helped
Finish with a longer run at race pace rather than qualifying pace, since that's closer to what you'll actually need on race day

sections.p: With less downforce dialed in, the ~MOZA R9 telegraphs the Kink's edge-of-grip feeling more honestly than at a high-downforce track — I keep FFB moderate so I can still feel the car go light without it becoming harsh.

I mention wheel feel specifically because Road America is a good example of how much a track's character can change what a 'good' FFB setting even means. A profile that feels great somewhere flat and smooth can feel either numb or harsh somewhere with real elevation change or bumps, and this track is one where I've had to actually revisit my base settings rather than assume they'd transfer.

sections.tip: If the Kink feels sketchy at first, lower your commitment gradually over a few laps rather than either avoiding it or sending it blind — this is a corner where confidence has to be earned, not assumed.

sections.h2: Mistakes I still see (and sometimes still make)

list: Lifting through the Kink out of nerves and getting run into from behind
Braking too late for Canada Corner and running wide onto the exit curbing
Getting impatient in the Carousel and adding throttle before the car has rotated

sections.p: What all of these mistakes have in common is that they're habits carried over from somewhere else — a different track, a different car, a different session — rather than something specific to Road America itself. The fix isn't usually a dramatic technique change, it's just deliberately unlearning the habit that doesn't apply here.

sections.h2: Race craft specifically at this track

sections.p: Single-lap pace and race pace at Road America aren't the same skill, and I'd be doing you a disservice if I only talked about qualifying laps. In traffic, the corners that felt straightforward in isolation often play out completely differently — a car ahead braking a fraction earlier than you expected, or a car alongside taking away the line you were planning to use. I try to build in a little more margin at the corners I've flagged above specifically because that's where a first-lap mistake compounds into an actual incident rather than just a slow lap.

None of this replaces seat time — track knowledge on iRacing comes from laps, not from reading about them. But knowing where the trouble spots are before you find them the hard way saves a few incident points along the way. If you're still dialing in your braking feel generally, I wrote up my notes on whether GT3 or GT4 suits you first separately, and it's worth reading alongside anything track-specific.

faqs.q: What's the hardest corner at Road America on iRacing?
faqs.a: Turn 5 (the Kink) tends to catch the most drivers, based on what I see in replays and incident reports.

faqs.q: Do I need a high-end wheelbase to learn Road America?
faqs.a: No — track knowledge and braking points transfer across wheel setups. A direct drive wheel like my ~MOZA R9 makes the feedback clearer, but it won't teach you the line by itself.

faqs.q: How many laps does it usually take to feel comfortable here?
faqs.a: It varies a lot by driver, but I'd budget a full practice session or two of focused laps before expecting genuine confidence, especially at a technical or blind-corner-heavy track.

faqs.q: Does setup matter more than driving line at this track?
faqs.a: Driving line first, always — a good setup makes a well-driven lap faster, but it won't fix a fundamentally wrong line or braking point.
